about.title: Scotts Valley Slip & Fall Claims
about.longDescription: Scotts Valley's mix of small retail centers, hillside walkways, and older sidewalks near Mt Hermon Road and Scotts Valley Drive creates plenty of everyday spots where a wet floor, cracked pavement, or poor lighting can lead to a serious fall. Under California law, a property owner or business isn't automatically responsible just because someone got hurt on their premises — the injured person generally has to show the owner knew, or reasonably should have known, about the hazard and didn't fix it or warn about it. That's why what happens in the minutes and days after a fall matters. Photos of the hazard, witness names, and a request to preserve any surveillance footage can make a real difference later. LawProactive connects Scotts Valley residents hurt in a fall with an independent attorney who can evaluate the notice issue, gather evidence, and explain your options — at no upfront cost to you.

items.title: Notice Is Everything
items.desc: California premises cases turn on whether the property owner knew or should have known about the hazard. An attorney can help identify evidence — like prior complaints or maintenance logs — that speaks directly to that notice requirement.

items.title: Time-Sensitive Evidence
items.desc: Surveillance footage at Scotts Valley shopping centers and businesses is often overwritten within days or weeks. Acting quickly to request preservation of that video can be critical to your claim.

items.title: Comparative Fault Doesn't Bar You
items.desc: California follows pure comparative fault, meaning you may still recover damages even if you were partly responsible for the fall. An independent attorney can help explain how that might apply to your specific situation.

items.question: How long do I have to file a slip and fall claim in Scotts Valley?
items.answer: Generally, California gives you two years from the date of the fall to file a premises liability lawsuit. That window can be shorter if a government entity owns or maintains the property, such as a public sidewalk or building. It's best to speak with an attorney early so important deadlines aren't missed.

items.question: What if I fell on public property in Scotts Valley, like a city sidewalk?
items.answer: Claims involving a government-owned property, such as a city-maintained walkway, follow different and often shorter deadlines than claims against private businesses. These claims may also require a special notice filed with the public entity before a lawsuit can proceed. An independent attorney can help sort out which rules apply to your situation.

items.question: Does it matter that I wasn't paying attention when I fell?
items.answer: Not necessarily. California's pure comparative fault rule means you can still pursue compensation even if you share some responsibility for the fall, though your recovery may be reduced by your share of fault. It's still worth having an attorney review the facts, including what the property owner knew about the hazard.
